### Problem: Russian doll envelopes {#sec-lis-p2-doll}

::: {.p-statement}
You have envelopes `envelopes[i] = [w, h]`. You may nest one inside another when both the width and the height are strictly smaller. You may not rotate an envelope. Return the maximum number of envelopes you can nest in one chain.

$1 \le n \le 10^5$. On $[[5, 4], [6, 4], [6, 7], [2, 3]]$ the answer is 3: $[2, 3] \subset [5, 4] \subset [6, 7]$. On $[[1, 1], [1, 1], [1, 1]]$ the answer is 1.

Source: [LC 354 · Russian Doll Envelopes](https://leetcode.com/problems/russian-doll-envelopes/){.solved difficulty="Hard"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
A wider envelope can only be outside a narrower one, so the width order is a legal order of the chain. After sorting by width, the only freedom left is the height, and the chain is an LIS on the heights. $[6, 4]$ has the same width as $[6, 7]$, so it must not extend that chain. Putting the taller envelope first inside the tie makes the later height smaller, and a strict LIS refuses it.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
- **Order.** Sort by width ascending, and by height descending when widths are equal.
- **State.** $end[i]$ = longest chain whose outermost envelope is the $i$-th in this order.
- **Transition.** $end[i] = 1 + \max\{end[j] : j < i,\ h[j] < h[i]\}$.
- **Answer.** $\max_i end[i]$. The $O(n \log n)$ form is the strict tails array on the heights.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Why the heights go down inside a tie"}
Take $[1, 1]$ and $[1, 2]$. Width ascending and height ascending yields heights $1, 2$, and a strict LIS reports 2. The envelopes do not nest. Height descending yields $2, 1$, and the LIS reports 1.

The same sort puts $[6, 7]$ before $[6, 4]$. The height sequence of the sample is $3, 4, 7, 4$. The second 4 does not extend 7. The chain of three is $3, 4, 7$, which is $[2, 3] \subset [5, 4] \subset [6, 7]$.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Recursion

::: {.form-next}
Sort first. `f(i)` is the longest chain whose outermost envelope is index `i` in that order. It extends an earlier envelope only when the height is strictly smaller. The answer is the best ending, not the last envelope.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("doll", "rec")
    assert str(final) == "3"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: doll-rec
def _dolls(env):
    return sorted(env, key=lambda e: (e[0], -e[1]))

def doll_rec(env):
    h = [e[1] for e in _dolls(env)]

    def f(i):
        best = 1
        for j in range(i):
            if h[j] < h[i]:
                best = max(best, 1 + f(j))
        return best

    return max(f(i) for i in range(len(h)))
```

##### C++

```cpp
int dollRec(int i, const vector<int>& h) {
    int best = 1;
    for (int j = 0; j < i; ++j)
        if (h[j] < h[i]) best = max(best, 1 + dollRec(j, h));
    return best;
}
```
:::

#### Memo

::: {.form-next}
The same recursion, with one stored length per envelope. There are `n` endings and each one scans the earlier envelopes.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("doll", "memo")
    assert str(final) == "3"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: doll-memo
def doll_memo(env):
    h = [e[1] for e in _dolls(env)]
    memo = [-1] * len(h)

    def f(i):
        if memo[i] < 0:
            best = 1
            for j in range(i):
                if h[j] < h[i]:
                    best = max(best, 1 + f(j))
            memo[i] = best
        return memo[i]

    return max(f(i) for i in range(len(h)))
```

##### C++

```cpp
int dollMemo(int i, const vector<int>& h, vector<int>& memo) {
    if (memo[i] >= 0) return memo[i];
    int best = 1;
    for (int j = 0; j < i; ++j)
        if (h[j] < h[i]) best = max(best, 1 + dollMemo(j, h, memo));
    return memo[i] = best;
}
```
:::

#### Table

::: {.form-next}
Fill the lengths from the left after the sort. The height test is the only compatibility test: the width order, including the descending tie, is already in the array.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("doll", "tab")
    assert str(final) == "3"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: doll-tab
def doll_tab(env):
    h = [e[1] for e in _dolls(env)]
    end = [1] * len(h)
    for i in range(len(h)):
        for j in range(i):
            if h[j] < h[i]:
                end[i] = max(end[i], end[j] + 1)
    return max(end)
```

##### C++

```cpp
int dollTab(vector<pair<int, int>> env) {
    sort(env.begin(), env.end(), [](auto& p, auto& q) {
        if (p.first != q.first) return p.first < q.first;
        return p.second > q.second;
    });
    int n = env.size();
    vector<int> end(n, 1);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i)
        for (int j = 0; j < i; ++j)
            if (env[j].second < env[i].second) end[i] = max(end[i], end[j] + 1);
    return *max_element(end.begin(), end.end());
}
```
:::

#### Tails

::: {.form-next}
The heights are an ordinary strict LIS after the sort. The tails array replaces the inner loop. $n = 10^5$ is this button. The length is the answer; there is nothing to reconstruct.
:::

```{python}

#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("doll", "tails")
    assert str(final) == "3"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: doll-tails
def doll_tails(env):
    return lis_tails([e[1] for e in _dolls(env)])[0]

sample = [[5, 4], [6, 4], [6, 7], [2, 3]]
assert doll_rec(sample) == doll_memo(sample) == doll_tab(sample) == doll_tails(sample) == 3
assert doll_tails([[1, 1], [1, 1], [1, 1]]) == 1
assert doll_tails([[1, 1], [1, 2]]) == 1
assert doll_tab([[4, 5], [4, 6], [6, 7], [2, 3], [1, 1]]) == doll_tails([[4, 5], [4, 6], [6, 7], [2, 3], [1, 1]])
```

##### C++

```cpp
int dollTails(vector<pair<int, int>> env) {
    sort(env.begin(), env.end(), [](auto& p, auto& q) {
        if (p.first != q.first) return p.first < q.first;
        return p.second > q.second;
    });
    vector<int> tails;
    for (auto& e : env) {
        int lo = 0, hi = tails.size();
        while (lo < hi) {
            int mid = (lo + hi) / 2;
            if (tails[mid] >= e.second) hi = mid;
            else lo = mid + 1;
        }
        if (lo == (int)tails.size()) tails.push_back(e.second);
        else tails[lo] = e.second;
    }
    return tails.size();
}
```
:::

:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Recursion** and **memoisation** are $O(n^2)$ after the sort, and the recursion is only for a short list. The **table** is $O(n^2)$. **Tails** is $O(n \log n)$. The sort is $O(n \log n)$ in every form. $n \le 10^5$ is the tails form.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- Every envelope equal: the answer is 1. The descending tie plus a strict comparison refuses the chain.
- One envelope: the answer is 1.
- A chain can end before the last envelope. $[6, 4]$ sits at the end of the sorted sample and does not extend the chain of three.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistakes"}
- Sorting both keys ascending. Equal widths with increasing heights become a fake chain. $[[1, 1], [1, 2]]$ must answer 1.
- Using $\le$ on the heights. The problem is strict in both dimensions. The descending tie is what makes a strict height test enforce a strict width test.
- Rotating an envelope. This problem does not allow it. The cuboid problem does.
:::

**Variants.** Pairs that chain when the right end is strictly left of the next left end sort by the right end, and the unweighted case is also the greedy earliest end: [LC 646 · Maximum Length of Pair Chain](https://leetcode.com/problems/maximum-length-of-pair-chain/){difficulty="Medium"}. Words that grow by one inserted letter sort by length, and the predecessor is a hash lookup of each deletion: [LC 1048 · Longest String Chain](https://leetcode.com/problems/longest-string-chain/){difficulty="Medium"}.
